memoryReview.evidence: covers/fog-of-conquest.jpg (legacy capture, direct image review unverified in this revision)
memoryReview.lesson: Its geographic field is the entire strategic object; Crown Laws instead keeps one bounded 5×7 stone tabletop and a fixed hand of decrees.

memoryReview.evidence: covers/zamazka.jpg (legacy capture, direct image review unverified in this revision)
memoryReview.lesson: Painting and canvas tools dominate ZAMAZKA; Crown Laws must show legal decisions before tools or flourishes, with pieces moving automatically.

references.observation: The Met documents medieval book covers using precious materials and strong geometric surfaces rather than floating interface ornaments.
references.principle: Use compact material boundaries to distinguish the legal decree object from its surrounding stone institution.
references.application: Rectangular parchment law cards use ink-like text and a thin stamped faction strip instead of illustrated backgrounds.
references.avoid: Do not reproduce specific manuscript pages, monograms, protected imagery or decorative initial drawings.

references.observation: V&A discusses Gothic objects crossing from architecture to three-dimensional sculpture with distinct material edges.
references.principle: A frame should behave like carved physical support around the royal game, not a generic translucent card.
references.application: The playfield uses a thick bevelled stone surround, measured cells and strong unbroken rectangular panel edges.
references.avoid: Avoid building an illegible ornamental cathedral facade over the usable interactive board.

references.observation: The British Library records the Lansdowne Psalter with framed miniatures and deliberate gold, orange and blue distinctions.
references.principle: Restrained colored detail can communicate function while retaining the seriousness of medieval record keeping.
references.application: The North and South counters have separate blue and red material rings; bronze focuses primary decree confirmation.
references.avoid: Do not borrow actual manuscript miniatures or treat decorative colors as interchangeable game-state labels.

concepts.medium: Hand-authored full-figure SVG sprite atlas and relief/carved decorative SVG on a strictly flat board, physical paper and stone panels composed in CSS
concepts.composition: Six visibly differentiated pieces occupy the 5x7 court; five laws are bound in an ivory codex on desktop and arranged into seals on mobile; decree choice resembles an illustrated folded folio
concepts.interaction: Select a decree once, inspect any existing rule without losing the selection, compare current and proposed world laws in a single manuscript inspector, then intentionally preview, confirm or unselect. The inspector has no authority to modify match state.
concepts.motion: Wax-arrow indicators mark a proposed category while leaving the standing law legible. One compact codex sheet folds in place without moving the board; reduced-motion removes its opening movement.
concepts.rationale: Replace repetitive circular portrait tokens and generic cards with character silhouettes and one consistent material grammar.

concepts.medium: A bespoke canvas renderer with hand-placed sculptural pseudo-relief and carved ornamental individual miniatures.
concepts.composition: The battlefield fills the scene as one altar stone while tiny side plaques hide available current laws and cards.
concepts.interaction: Players drag embossed coins from an arc surrounding the board into a central slot to submit hidden commands.
concepts.motion: Heavily eased rotations and carved-piece swells would make each resolution ceremonial and comparatively slow.
concepts.rationale: Its strong theatrical model introduces gesture-dependent controls that would bury readable decrees on a small screen.

concepts.medium: Multi-page CSS folio instrument with stitched side margins, codex gutters and text-first ink panels.
concepts.composition: Each gameplay layer is a separate full-screen folio: board page, law book page, decree page and chronicle page.
concepts.interaction: Users flip between folios to examine individual acts and apply a decree from a compact bottom page tab.
concepts.motion: A page-turn sequence and layered parchment scroll would organize navigation around document transitions.
concepts.rationale: It makes room for long legal prose but repeatedly obscures the shared board precisely when laws are being evaluated.

selection.reason: The law comparison is a single reversible card-to-world action rather than two disconnected rectangular information panels. The standing public law and private decree are separated by an engraved wax transition.

rejected.reason: Full sculptural or 2.5D tabletop changes the viewing perspective and obscures legal state, adding art and interaction complexity without aiding the strategy.
Multiple separate page-flip screens force players to stop watching the board whenever they inspect the active laws or decree hand, undermining rapid decision-making.

tools.reason: Original browser HTML and CSS provide all board, token, material and feedback geometry without generated SVG or picture tiles.
A deterministic Node image routine draws the product crown onto an isolated pixel buffer and serializes one PNG for the app icon.
Editable native SVG sources and self-contained identical runtime SVG exports are committed; full Inkscape PNG and hash-index build is not yet verified in this connected environment.
tools.fallback: Continue using the published identical self-contained SVG sources directly inside the local application until native Inkscape exports and the checked Forge index can be committed.

risks: At 390 pixel widths the hand needs to remain accessible without the current law ledger hiding board controls.
At tablet landscape sizes the side ledger and board must not obstruct the confirmation action.
The full Art Forge 2D PNG/index rebuild is pending. The build manifest must not be activated with missing files.
Ensure previous film timers cannot repaint or override newer online turns; a generation token invalidates stale callbacks.
Confirm WebKit audio is gesture-gated; unavailable audio devices must not interrupt the phase timeline.
Counsel Vision is deliberately counterfactual: the opponent is assumed to leave all laws unchanged; its future hidden decree cannot be inferred. Keep this notice visible.
The preview stores detached snapshots only, never adjusting cards, crowns, network messages, or active turns; avoid accidentally rendering it into a persistent match state.
Clipboard copying may be blocked by browser permissions; never show success unless the Promise resolves.
Victory must reflect actual winner and current viewer; avoid showing the same congratulations to the losing online player.
Inspecting a standing law or figure must not clear selectedCardId; this is critical when comparing several categories in multiplayer.
The comparison and selected-decree controls must not become visible during hidden hot-seat handoff or while another player is deciding.
comparisons: Capture initial menu and compare type/edges to former hero layout to verify absence of recovered assets.
Capture settled board and chosen decree and compare with prior sprite sheet render for readability and dimensional correctness.

comparisons.before: Legacy instant jump from one board state to the final state after a complete turn.
comparisons.after: Successive snapshots from the actual game-engine phases show precisely which actor moved and when, with a control to skip.

comparisons.before: 0.6 forecast jumps directly between initial and resulting boards; changed actors are hard to trace.
comparisons.after: 0.7 forecast allows nine-step chronological inspection, exact movement trails, side-by-side scenario switching and alternate translucent actor silhouettes.

comparisons.before: Flat text waiting room, one static result modal and dry rules list.
comparisons.after: Illustrated two-chair foyer, different win/loss ceremonies with actual result and chronicle, interactive five-chapter manuscript tutorial.

comparisons.before: Tapping any standing law deselected the player's hand, and the selected decree detail appeared separately inside the tray.
comparisons.after: A single overlay compares the active public law with the proposed private decree; switching inspections preserves the choice and leaves the mobile board stationary.
